articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Jodie Sweetin Breaks Down ’90s Nostalgia and What She Misses Most from the Days Before Cellphones
articles.content:
Jodie Sweetin is best known as a ’90s TV star—and she’s leaning into the nostalgia. She rose to fame at 5 years old, playing Stephanie Tanner on Full House, one of the marquee shows on ABC’s TGIF lineup, and resurrected Steph for Netflix’s Fuller House, which ran from 2016 to 2020. And while she most recently starred as the Sorcerer Queen on Vampirina: Teenage Vampire on Disney+, earlier this year she also appeared on HGTV’s Totally ’90s House alongside other ’90s icons, including Melissa Joan Hart and Brian Austin Green.
Which makes it only fitting that Reader’s Digest caught up with Sweetin at an exclusive reveal of the Club Wyndham Holiday Rewind Suite at Club Wyndham Midtown 45 in New York City. Stepping into the suite is like taking a time machine back to the 1990s: The walls are covered in wood paneling and retro-patterned wallpaper, and a boxy TV comes complete with a VCR and VHS tapes to go with it. The magnet-covered fridge is filled with bottles of SunnyD and Little Hug Fruit Barrels in a rainbow of neon colors. And in the bedroom, you’ll be greeted with ’90s magazine covers, a boombox, CDs from the ’90s, and glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling.
It’s a whole vibe—and so is Sweetin, who we had a blast chatting with. Read on to find out what she misses most about the decade, how you can add a little ’90s nostalgia to your life and which tradition she thinks the holidays just wouldn’t be the same without.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
This interview took place on Oct. 8, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity.
Reader’s Digest: The ’90s are having a moment. Why do you think people are so nostalgic when they look back at the decade?
Jodie Sweetin: I think people are nostalgic for a life that was a little slower and not as distracted. Even when we’re not on our phones, we don’t realize how much the constant humming and notifications get to us. It’s always something. I think people really miss slowing down and taking time to [do things like] rewind a VHS tape—literally those sorts of things.
I also think the ’90s are having a resurgence because those of us who lived through the ’90s as teenagers are now in charge of things and we’re like, “We want to see the ’90s!” And it’s pretty awesome. It was a great decade.
Reader’s Digest: You spent so much of your childhood on Full House. What’s something about being a kid in the ’90s that you think younger people might have a hard time understanding today?
Jodie Sweetin: Oh, man. I feel like young people didn’t have as much of an impact as they do today. I don’t know if it’s social media or whatever, but with kids and teens these days, I feel like we have a little more respect for what they have to say and what they think. I remember in the ’90s, it was like, “Ah, you’re a kid, you don’t know.” I feel like we’ve tried to give our youth a little more of a voice.
Reader’s Digest: For sure. I was never asked where we wanted to go on vacation.
Jodie Sweetin: Right. Or even just conversations. Our parents’ generation still wasn’t quite as open about talking about stuff, and I think our generation has really been the opposite of that with our kids. We have very open, honest conversations about life.
I do a lot of work in that space with young people, around drugs and recovery, and it’s surprising how many people are like, “Oh, I don’t have to talk to them until seventh grade.” And you’re like, “Oh, honey, they’re on the internet.” They know things. [Editor’s note: Sweetin is an advocate for addiction recovery and wrote about her own experience with addiction and recovery in her autobiography, UnSweetined.]
Reader’s Digest: Stephanie Tanner’s “How rude!” became one of the greatest pop-culture catchphrases of all time. Did you ever say it at the wrong time?
Jodie Sweetin: I don’t think so. Actually, there have been times when it was the absolute right time and I didn’t say it. I regret those moments more—like, “Oh, that would have been a great ‘How rude!’ moment.” I always say “How rude!” is going to be on my tombstone. That feels appropriate.
Reader’s Digest: What do you think would make Stephanie say it today?
Jodie Sweetin: I think Steph would say that about people who don’t stick up for those who have less of a voice than they do. Steph was always about the underdog, and she was always about speaking up for people. I think that’s exactly what she’d do today—be like, “No, we’re still not going to do that.” I always liked Steph for that.
Reader’s Digest: It sounds like maybe you’ve incorporated that into your career.
Jodie Sweetin: Steph and I are very similar sometimes. When you’re a kid on a show, they really write who you are a lot of the time, because it’s much easier to figure out who a kid is and write to that than to try to make them something else. So in many ways over the years, Steph and I just melded into one another. But I was always really proud that Steph fought for the underdog, for people who maybe couldn’t fight for themselves or couldn’t fight as hard for themselves. I respect that about her.
Reader’s Digest: Let’s switch gears. When you think about the holidays when you were growing up, what’s one tradition or memory that immediately takes you back?
Jodie Sweetin: Every year, my mom and I and our family friends, another mom and daughter, would drive all over the place to look at Christmas lights. I still love doing that. But this was back in the day. There was no Google Maps. You had to hear it by word of mouth, like, “Hey, this neighborhood is really good.” We’d go out all night and bring a little thermos of hot chocolate, roll the windows down and drive through neighborhoods looking at lights. It was one of my favorite things.
Reader’s Digest: Are there any holiday traditions you loved as a kid that you still do or that you’ve reinvented for your own daughters?
Jodie Sweetin: Christmas pajamas. My mom always did them for me, even back in the ’90s. Especially back in the ’90s. The one year she didn’t was when I’d first moved out and had my own house. She was like, “You don’t need Christmas pajamas.” And I was like, “I absolutely do, because now it’s not Christmas.”
So Christmas pajamas are a must, and I did it with my girls [Zoie and Beatrix]. We always did the matching jammies, but now that they’re 18 and 16, fine, we won’t match. It’s got to be cute. I’m like, OK, not flannel and long-sleeved.
Reader’s Digest: What have we gained or lost in the ways we celebrate the holidays now versus how we celebrated them in the ’90s?
Jodie Sweetin: What we’ve gained is the ability to connect with people on a larger scale, but I think we’ve lost the ability to connect on a small scale, in a one-on-one, intimate conversation. So much of our life has become online, for our followers or whoever. In the ’90s, you’d just go hang out with a friend, and it didn’t matter if you took a picture of it. I think we’ve lost the ability to be present, despite gaining all these things that are supposed to keep us better connected. We have a wider connection ability but less of an intimate connection ability, if that makes sense.
Reader’s Digest: This is going to be the hardest question yet. When you walked into the Holiday Rewind Suite, what was the first thing you noticed?
Jodie Sweetin: Oh, the first thing I noticed when I walked in? I thought you were going to say the first thing I said, and I was like, well, I can’t use that.
The first thing I noticed was the [wood] paneling. That and the wallpaper really took me back. It reminds me of every friend’s house I went to, every family member’s house. They all had the wood paneling. And the china! My mom has that [holiday] china. She used it one time, when I was, like, 11. And we still have all the dishes—a full service for 12!
Reader’s Digest: And that’ll be yours someday.
Jodie Sweetin: Oh, no. She’s already trying to pass stuff down, and I was like, “Look, lady, I love you, but … mm-mm. This isn’t mine.” It’s beautiful, but I’m better at making reservations than dinner.
But this suite—all of it, the carpet, the seats, the chairs, every moment in here—really took me back to easy, simpler times. A little more analog, as the young people say these days. I don’t think people have any idea just how cool it is. It’ll be really fun.
The Club Wyndham Holiday Rewind Suite at Club Wyndham Midtown 45 in New York City is available to book from Nov. 6, 2026, through Jan. 4, 2027. Visit ClubWyndham.com/HolidayRewind for more info.

articles.title: Burger King Is Bringing Back Its Fan-Favorite Advent Calendar—But This Year’s Version Has a Surprising Twist
articles.content:
Advent calendars have come a long way from the days of opening a tiny cardboard door to find a piece of chocolate. Now, you can count down to Old Saint Nick with everything from high-end beauty products to mini bottles of wine. And if you have kids, there’s an Advent calendar for just about every toy, movie character and viral trend. My fellow Nee-Doh-hunting moms can certainly relate here.
Just when we thought we’d seen it all, Burger King got in on the holiday action, releasing its very first Advent calendar in 2024. And this year, the fast-food giant has put a new twist on the festive tradition. Burger King is bringing back its popular Advent calendar for the third year in a row, and the fast-food giant says this year’s version is its best one yet.
Unlike the burger chain’s previous calendars, which were stuffed with assorted goodies like plush toys, fanny packs and beanies, the newest edition comes with everything you need to build your very own miniature Burger King restaurant! And yes, it’s as adorable as it sounds.
The first thing you need to know is that Burger King’s 2026 Advent calendar doesn’t follow the usual 24-day countdown. This one features 12 doors, each hiding a miniature piece of the restaurant.
According to the company’s Nov. 5 announcement, the collectibles include a Whopper in its new packaging, chicken nuggets with sauce, french fries, an ice cream cone, a soda fountain, a kitchen prep station and the King’s Booth. There’s even a tiny employee, a customer wearing a crown, a Christmas tree and a reindeer. By the time you open the final door, you’ll have everything you need to fully assemble a miniature Burger King restaurant.
But wait—that’s not all! There’s one extra surprise waiting behind door No. 12—a QR code unlocking a $5 digital Burger King offer for eligible Royal Perks members.
Here’s where things get tricky.
If you’re hoping to snag one of these mini restaurants, you’ll need a little patience and possibly some luck. The calendars were originally scheduled to go on sale Monday, Nov. 16, but the first drop was delayed. So for everyone just finding out about this cute little holiday gem, you’re not too late to the party. A Burger King spokesperson told Reader’s Digest on Nov. 17 that the company was experiencing website issues and hoped to have the calendars available on Wednesday, Nov. 18, two days later than originally advertised.
View this post on Instagram
Burger King originally planned to release 110 calendars each day through Nov. 20, with each batch going live at 12 p.m. ET. Each Advent calendar costs $19.54, a sweet little nod to the year the fast-food chain was founded, and will be available exclusively at BkAdventCalendar.com.
If past years are any indication, these little restaurants won’t stick around for long. The chain’s previous two calendars sold out in less than five minutes.

articles.title: Why Do We Clink Glasses When Making a Toast?
articles.content:
Whether you’re celebrating at a wedding reception, casually hanging out with friends or ringing in the new year, someone will eventually raise a glass and say, “Cheers!” Before you know it, everyone is reaching across the table to clink glasses. I’ve done it on plenty of occasions, of course, but my favorite toasts have been a little less traditional: clinking my champagne flute (filled with “Aunt Jo Juice”) against my nephew’s sippy cup. He was delighted to be included, and honestly, it felt just as celebratory as any other toast.
That’s the funny thing about clinking glasses: It doesn’t really matter what’s in the glass—or even whether it’s a glass at all. There’s something about that little tap and familiar tinkling noise that makes a moment feel special, as though everyone is part of a celebration.
But have you ever wondered, Why do people clink glasses in the first place? How did this little social ritual get started, and is there more to it than just that satisfying sound? As it turns out, the history is worth raising a glass to.
To explore the origins and etiquette of this custom, I consulted Rémy Duthille, PhD, a professor at Université Bordeaux Montaigne in France who researches the history of drinking and toasting, along with etiquette experts Ziying Zhou and Myka Meier. Together, they help separate historical fact from popular myth—and offer advice on how to raise a glass with confidence. Cheers to that!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, holidays, grammar, humor, travel and tech all week long.
If you’ve ever heard that clinking glasses originated to prevent poisoning or scare away evil spirits, you’re not alone. But Duthille urges caution. “I do not know if those popular theories are true,” he says. “I never found any evidence of them.”
Still, they’re fun stories. Let’s take a closer look.
One popular explanation claims that people began clinking glasses during the Middle Ages to guard against poisoned drinks. According to the story, diners struck their vessels hard enough for liquid to splash between them, making poisoning a risky proposition.
The problem? The logistics are questionable. There would be no guarantee that liquid would transfer between glasses, let alone in a quantity sufficient to make a difference. There’s also the question of timing. As Duthille points out, “clinking glasses supposes the existence of glasses,” and drinking from individual glasses (as opposed to communal bowls) didn’t become popular in Britain until the late 17th and early 18th centuries. So the familiar image of people touching drinking glasses is not something we can project onto every historical banquet.
Another explanation suggests that during the Middle Ages, people clinked glasses in the hope that the noise would frighten any evil spirits lurking nearby. Perhaps that’s because the noise resembled church bells, which demons would avoid (obvi). It’s a colorful idea, but again, Duthille notes, there’s no convincing historical evidence that this is how the custom began.
Here’s a more romantic explanation. Drinking already engages four of our senses. We see the drink, feel the glass, smell its contents and taste what’s inside. Clinking adds the fifth sense: hearing.
It’s a lovely thought, especially when you’re sharing a special bottle with friends. But Duthille isn’t convinced. “The idea that clinking matters because drinking is an experience of the five senses is beautiful,” he says, “but I do not think it is historically grounded.”
The honest answer is that historians can’t point to one definitive origin or say exactly when clinking individual glasses became part of the tradition of raising a drink in someone’s honor. They can, however, trace the history of toasting and the popularity of clinking.
To understand how the familiar “Cheers!” ritual evolved, it helps to start with the custom of toasting itself, which goes back thousands of years to the ancient Greeks, Romans, Egyptians and Persians. The Roman Senate reportedly required citizens to drink to Emperor Augustus’s health at every meal, according to Toastmasters International.
And here’s a fun fact about where the word toast came from: The Romans are believed to have added toasted bread crumbs to wine to reduce its acidity. The word is thought to derive from the Latin tostus, meaning “to dry up” or “scorch.” The Oxford English Dictionary dates toast, meaning “to propose a drink in someone’s honor,” to 1699.
By the 18th century, toasting had become a familiar feature of social occasions in Britain. People raised their glasses to honor public figures, celebrate important events and express admiration or affection. Toasting became so established that dedicated toastmasters helped organize formal occasions and ensure everyone had a chance to offer a toast. One of the earliest books devoted to the subject, The Royal Toastmaster, was published in London in 1791.
A particularly charming example of a toast becoming a lasting tradition is the Burns Supper, an annual celebration honoring Scottish poet Robert Burns. The first recorded supper took place on July 21, 1801, five years after the poet’s death. Nine of his friends gathered at Burns Cottage in Alloway, Scotland, to remember him, enjoy a meal and recite his work. They also raised a toast to his memory. The gathering inspired Burns Night, now celebrated worldwide around the poet’s birthday on Jan. 25.
The tradition of toasting continued to flourish in the 19th century. In the United States, the period from approximately 1880 to 1920 has even been described as a golden age of toasting. Toast books and pamphlets became popular, newspapers published columns about toasts, and prominent writers contributed their own witty and sentimental offerings. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raising a glass together had become a familiar feature of celebrations and social gatherings on both sides of the Atlantic.

articles.summary:
Whether you’re celebrating at a wedding reception, casually hanging out with friends or ringing in the new year, someone will eventually raise a glass and say, “Cheers!” Before you know it, everyone is reaching across the table to clink glasses. I’ve done it on plenty of occasions, of course, but my favorite toasts have been a little less traditional: clinking my champagne flute (filled with “Aunt Jo Juice”) against my nephew’s sippy cup. He was delighted to be included, and honestly, it felt just as celebratory as any other toast.

That’s the funny thing about clinking glasses: It doesn’t really matter what’s in the glass—or even whether it’s a glass at all. There’s something about that little tap and familiar tinkling noise that makes a moment feel special, as though everyone is part of a celebration.

But have you ever wondered, Why do people clink glasses in the first place? How did this little social ritual get started, and is there more to it than just that satisfying sound? As it turns out, the history is worth raising a glass to.

To explore the origins and etiquette of this custom, I consulted Rémy Duthille, PhD, a professor at Université Bordeaux Montaigne in France who researches the history of drinking and toasting, along with etiquette experts Ziying Zhou and Myka Meier. Together, they help separate historical fact from popular myth—and offer advice on how to raise a glass with confidence. Cheers to that!

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, holidays, grammar, humor, travel and tech all week long.

What are the theories behind why people clink glasses?

If you’ve ever heard that clinking glasses originated to prevent poisoning or scare away evil spirits, you’re not alone. But Duthille urges caution. “I do not know if those popular theories are true,” he says. “I never found any evidence of them.”

Still, they’re fun stories. Let’s take a closer look.

The poisoned-drink theory

One popular explanation claims that people began clinking glasses during the Middle Ages to guard against poisoned drinks. According to the story, diners struck their vessels hard enough for liquid to splash between them, making poisoning a risky proposition.

The problem? The logistics are questionable. There would be no guarantee that liquid would transfer between glasses, let alone in a quantity sufficient to make a difference. There’s also the question of timing. As Duthille points out, “clinking glasses supposes the existence of glasses,” and drinking from individual glasses (as opposed to communal bowls) didn’t become popular in Britain until the late 17th and early 18th centuries. So the familiar image of people touching drinking glasses is not something we can project onto every historical banquet.

The evil-spirits theory

Another explanation suggests that during the Middle Ages, people clinked glasses in the hope that the noise would frighten any evil spirits lurking nearby. Perhaps that’s because the noise resembled church bells, which demons would avoid (obvi). It’s a colorful idea, but again, Duthille notes, there’s no convincing historical evidence that this is how the custom began.

The five-senses theory

Here’s a more romantic explanation. Drinking already engages four of our senses. We see the drink, feel the glass, smell its contents and taste what’s inside. Clinking adds the fifth sense: hearing.

It’s a lovely thought, especially when you’re sharing a special bottle with friends. But Duthille isn’t convinced. “The idea that clinking matters because drinking is an experience of the five senses is beautiful,” he says, “but I do not think it is historically grounded.”

So why do we clink glasses?

The honest answer is that historians can’t point to one definitive origin or say exactly when clinking individual glasses became part of the tradition of raising a drink in someone’s honor. They can, however, trace the history of toasting and the popularity of clinking.

Toasting goes way back

To understand how the familiar “Cheers!” ritual evolved, it helps to start with the custom of toasting itself, which goes back thousands of years to the ancient Greeks, Romans, Egyptians and Persians. The Roman Senate reportedly required citizens to drink to Emperor Augustus’s health at every meal, according to Toastmasters International.

And here’s a fun fact about where the word toast came from: The Romans are believed to have added toasted bread crumbs to wine to reduce its acidity. The word is thought to derive from the Latin tostus, meaning “to dry up” or “scorch.” The Oxford English Dictionary dates toast, meaning “to propose a drink in someone’s honor,” to 1699.

The practice becomes widespread

By the 18th century, toasting had become a familiar feature of social occasions in Britain. People raised their glasses to honor public figures, celebrate important events and express admiration or affection. Toasting became so established that dedicated toastmasters helped organize formal occasions and ensure everyone had a chance to offer a toast. One of the earliest books devoted to the subject, The Royal Toastmaster, was published in London in 1791.

A particularly charming example of a toast becoming a lasting tradition is the Burns Supper, an annual celebration honoring Scottish poet Robert Burns. The first recorded supper took place on July 21, 1801, five years after the poet’s death. Nine of his friends gathered at Burns Cottage in Alloway, Scotland, to remember him, enjoy a meal and recite his work. They also raised a toast to his memory. The gathering inspired Burns Night, now celebrated worldwide around the poet’s birthday on Jan. 25.

The tradition of toasting continued to flourish in the 19th century. In the United States, the period from approximately 1880 to 1920 has even been described as a golden age of toasting. Toast books and pamphlets became popular, newspapers published columns about toasts, and prominent writers contributed their own witty and sentimental offerings. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raising a glass together had become a familiar feature of celebrations and social gatherings on both sides of the Atlantic.

Clinking develops alongside toasting

There’s no definitive historical record showing the exact year when clinking became an expected part of every toast. What we can say is that the practice became increasingly associated with the broader toasting ritual as individual glasses and social drinking traditions evolved.

Drinking from individual glasses—and making them part of a shared ritual—gained popularity in Britain during the 17th century. Duthille points to the appearance of specialized English toasting glasses in the 1680s. These vessels were sometimes made for individual clubs and societies, with designs that reflected the group’s identity and loyalties. By the 18th century, toasting was an established part of British social life, taking place in gentlemen’s clubs, political gatherings and private celebrations.

Then it gets solidified in literature

Literature offers another way to trace the custom’s growing familiarity. By the 19th century, writers were including clinking in their stories without needing to explain the gesture to readers. Here are a few notable mentions that strengthened the tradition:

  • One early example is Heinrich von Kleist’s comedy The Broken Pitcher. First performed in 1808, the play includes a scene in which one character urges the others, “Clink glasses now!”
  • Charles Dickens offers another example in Dombey and Son (1846–48). When young Walter Gills celebrates a new beginning with his uncle, the two clink glasses as they drink to each other’s good fortune. They do it again when Walter proposes a toast to his uncle. The moment is affectionate, turning a simple drink into a shared expression of pride and goodwill.
  • Gustave Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1856) includes a quieter example. Emma offers Charles a glass of liqueur, pours one for herself and the two touch glasses before drinking. Though not a grand celebration or formal toast, it shows the gesture being used in an ordinary, intimate exchange.
  • In a scene from Alexandre Dumas’s The Whites and the Blues (1867), several men clink their glasses while drinking to the health of the Republic. The moment takes an unfortunate turn when one man’s glass breaks from the impact, but it offers a vivid example of clinking as part of a public toast.
  • Toasting continued to appear in early 20th-century fiction. In James Joyce’s “A Little Cloud,” published in Dubliners (1914), two old friends meet in a bar and clink glasses as they drink to “old times and old acquaintance.”
  • William J. Locke’s The Wonderful Year (1916) offers a more celebratory scene: At a French cafe, a group welcomes a young man home from military service by clinking champagne glasses and drinking to his honor.

Today, of course, clinking glasses remains a visual shorthand for celebration, camaraderie and shared milestones. Whether on the page or the screen, that familiar little clink still signals a moment worth raising a glass to.

What are the rules of clinking glasses?

Whatever its origins, clinking glasses has become a familiar part of celebrations. But are there any rules to getting it right? Here are a few common etiquette questions.

Is it rude to clink glasses filled with water?

Not necessarily, though some cultures frown on it. The Germans believe raising a glass with water is bad luck. And in Spain, toasting with water is said to bring seven years of bad luck—particularly in the bedroom.

Meier says these are just superstitions, not universal rules. “From a modern etiquette perspective, it’s perfectly acceptable to toast with water or another nonalcoholic beverage,” she says. Zhou similarly emphasizes respecting those who choose not to drink alcohol, suggesting alternatives such as alcohol-free sparkling wine.

Duthille notes that alcohol’s historical association with toasting may stem partly from beliefs in its healing properties and wine’s religious significance in Christian communion.

Is it bad luck to clink an empty glass?

The ancient Romans reportedly believed raising an empty glass negated the good wishes in a toast, signaling that you were entering a friendship or celebration with empty intentions. Yes, it’s another superstition, but why tempt fate, right?

Zhou recommends having something in your glass. If you’ve finished your drink, Meier suggests simply raising the empty glass without pretending to drink.

Should you make eye contact when clinking glasses?

Yes. “Eye contact is a lovely way to show respect and acknowledge the person you’re celebrating with,” Meier says.

Zhou adds that a superstition in Germany and France warns that avoiding eye contact during a toast brings seven years of bad luck, specifically in the bedroom. Yep, that special brand of bad luck again!

How hard should you clink glasses?

“The golden rule is to clink gently,” Meier says. Delicate glassware, particularly crystal and thin-stemmed wine glasses, can chip or break. Pro tip: Zhou recommends aiming for the widest part of a wine glass’ bowl rather than its fragile rim.

Meier also advises against reaching awkwardly across the table. There’s no need to clink with everyone individually. Simply raising your glass and making eye contact is perfectly acceptable.

When is it appropriate to clink glasses?

Of course, clinking is common at weddings, birthdays, anniversaries and other celebrations, and people do it in plenty of casual settings too. However, in very formal situations, Meier says, “I would only clink glasses if my host or someone actively clinked.”

The key is to always be mindful of local customs and follow your host’s lead. Zhou notes that at formal state banquets and royal events in the U.K. and Europe, guests may simply raise their glasses without touching. In China, toasting can happen throughout a meal, and returning a toast is generally expected. When toasting someone older or more senior in China, she adds, it’s customary to lower your glass so its rim sits below theirs.

Ultimately, a toast is about celebrating a person or moment, not necessarily touching glasses. Whether you clink, raise your drink or simply smile, what matters is sharing the moment. We’ll drink to that!

About the experts

  • Rémy Duthille is a professor of British Studies at Université Bordeaux Montaigne in France who specializes in British political history and sociability during the 18th and 19th centuries. His research explores how drinking, dining and toasting shape political identities and social relationships.
  • Myka Meier is an internationally recognized etiquette expert, the founder of Beaumont Etiquette, the co-founder of The Plaza Hotel Finishing Program and the author of Modern Etiquette Made Easy and Business Etiquette Made Easy. Trained in London under a former member of the British Royal Household and at Switzerland’s Institut Villa Pierrefeu, she specializes in social, dining and business etiquette, as well as international protocol.
  • Ziying Zhou is an international etiquette expert and the founder of Berkeley Etiquette. Following a decade in investment and corporate banking, she transitioned into etiquette coaching, blending her global experiences with training at Switzerland’s renowned Institut Villa Pierrefeu. Her tailored coaching aims to enhance her clients’ confidence, communication skills and cross-cultural understanding.

articles.title: Princess Kate Revealed the Household Chore She Enjoys Doing with William, and It’s Shockingly Normal—And Sweet!
articles.content:
As someone who lives a decidedly “normal” life, the thought of living like a royal is very appealing. Let’s be honest: If given the chance, most of us would go all-in on the fancy, over-the-top perks afforded to us as a member of the monarchy. (No judgment here!)
But William and Kate, who have the literal keys to the kingdom, want the opposite. They have always emphasized their desire for normalcy, especially when it comes to their home life. So Kate’s recent revelation that she and her husband love doing a certain household chore together should come as no surprise … though it still kind of does, since most of us hate this particular task.
So what are the Prince and Princess of Wales doing behind closed doors? Read on to find out the details, along with how the rest of the Windsor clan keeps it royally real. Well, sometimes, anyway.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royals, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The dishes! Princess Kate enjoys getting the pots, pans and dishes squeaky-clean—and Prince William gets in on the action too. In fact, they’re a “good double act,” which is just about the sweetest thing we’ve heard about these two lovebirds. “I love washing up. I really do,” she said during a visit to a community lunch club for the elderly in September. “[William] does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved.”
The family primarily lives in eight-bedroom Forest Lodge in Windsor, but they also have a 10-bedroom country retreat in Sandringham, Norfolk, called Anmer Hall. By all accounts, the Wales clan’s home life is very normal and down-to-earth, with the children expected to set the table, clear their plates and tidy up. “It would surprise people to see how ordinary things are at home. There’s no special treatment,” a source told the Mirror in 2024. “The children are still expected to do their chores and to muck in.”
Yes and no. They could have staff at their beck and call if they wanted, but Kate has always wanted her children’s upbringing to be as normal as possible. So when they moved from Kensington Palace to Windsor in 2022, the royal couple opted not to have any live-in staff. Their loyal nanny, Maria Teresa Turrion Borrallo, came with them, but she lives nearby, as do other staff, such as housekeepers and gardeners. But there’s no valet for William, or any ladies-in-waiting for Kate. And the kids eat normal foods like pizza, mac and cheese, and salad—and even help make their own meals.
It’s a far cry from how the older generations of royals lived. William was privy to his family’s personal chef when he grew up in Kensington Palace, with ice cream available whenever he wanted it. (His favorite was apparently Häagen-Dazs chocolate chip.) And get this: When King Charles was Prince of Wales and broke his arm at a polo match in 1990, his aide Michael Fawcett famously squeezed toothpaste on his toothbrush. He was 41 at the time, in case you were wondering, and yeah, we’ll just leave it at that.
Plenty, to be honest! After all, it would be pretty challenging to try to function as a working royal without any assistants or nannies. Naturally, William and Kate do have lots of staff—they just don’t live with them, and the couple perform some of the “normal” tasks of everyday life themselves, like grocery shopping and cooking.
According to The Royal Household Sovereign Grant Report for 2026, William and Kate employ 74 staff. This includes private secretaries, press teams and finance, admin and travel teams, as well as household staff like housekeepers and gardeners. The couple has previously advertised for a housekeeper and assistant, with accommodations included. No word on whether the couple adheres to the strict royal cleaning test that the palace’s head of staff recruitment gives to prospective hires, though!
Yes, plenty of royals like to get their hands dirty—even the King.

He revealed she makes dinners of “scrambled eggs, fresh mince from the local butcher, fruit and [vegetables] from the garden.” Camilla often heads to her private home, Ray Mill House, on the weekends when she wants some normalcy.
  • King Charles: While he might not get the vacuum out, the king is a gardening aficionado. His gardens at Highgrove are famous, and he recently revived the ones at Sandringham Estate as well. “As a child, my sister and I were given a little plot at Buckingham Palace at the back of the border for growing vegetables,” he said. “But it’s not until you have somewhere of your own that it becomes more possible.” And yes, he does the digging. “I notice things and weed or prune bits off. I’m sure most people come here and think I don’t do anything. But I do.”

articles.title: Here’s Why Everyone Is Talking About SNL’s “Sister” Skit—And Why Brothers Might Get a Talking-To at Thanksgiving This Year
articles.content: Holidays are the time for celebrating with family, catching up with loved ones and, if your family is anything like mine, discussing serious current events and buzzy pop-culture moments while we lie around in our PJs watching giant balloon animals. This Thanksgiving, those topics will no doubt include the election, the latest hit movies and one of our favorite shows, Saturday Night Live. My brother and I watched SNL religiously growing up, along with other late-night staples like Letterman and SCTV, so we’re always ready to argue over the relative merits of particular seasons. Well, these brother-sister dynamics might be put to the test this year, because SNL just dropped its most polarizing and hilarious sketch in years. If you haven’t heard about the latest skit, “Sister,” we have the entire thing below. Depending on your perspective, you may laugh nervously, nod vigorously or cry knowingly at the very real situation SNL pokes fun at. Read on for details on the outrageous sketch that’s taking over your social media feed right now and will likely come up at Thanksgiving dinner. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long. The skit takes the form of a parody infomercial, with host John Mulaney addressing the camera like he’s about to sell you Medicare Part B. Over a backdrop of scenes of his elderly father, played by Tommy Brennan, Mulaney says he loves his dad and doesn’t want to see him go to a nursing home. And live-in care is expensive! “That’s when I heard about Sister,” he says to the camera. “Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder-care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” To activate, all Mulaney has to do is text: “Dad fell.” Soon, cast member Jane Wickline shows up at their father’s house with a roller bag after quitting her job and breaking her lease. Other cast members, including Andrew Dismukes and Keenan Thompson, speak to the camera about how much they love their moms, but that doesn’t mean they want to help them in the bathroom or learn about their “confusing” medicines. Sister doesn’t either, “but she will, whereas I won’t,” Dismukes says. For brothers, it’s a win-win: “Now I don’t have to worry about my dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it,” Mulaney says. “And I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do.” This skit hit a nerve, to say the least. Long-suffering, real-life “Sisters” took to social media to say they finally feel seen, while brothers and other siblings defended their own situations, which you know nothing about thank you very much! Sister partners, who also make an appearance in the skit, also related to this modern commentary on caregiving. “Speaking as someone who inadvertently found himself in the role of ‘Sister’s Husband,’ I can attest that this video is 100% accurate,” said someone on the official SNL YouTube channel. Very. Studies broadly support the idea that daughters are more likely than sons to take on caregiving roles for aging parents. According to a 2025 study by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 61% of caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men. One particularly biting part of the skit touches on well-worn societal expectations of daughters. Mikey Day plays a doctor (and author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care), who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours.” And in fact, studies bear this out. Holidays are the time for celebrating with family, catching up with loved ones and, if your family is anything like mine, discussing serious current events and buzzy pop-culture moments while we lie around in our PJs watching giant balloon animals. This Thanksgiving, those topics will no doubt include the election, the latest hit movies and one of our favorite shows, Saturday Night Live.

My brother and I watched SNL religiously growing up, along with other late-night staples like Letterman and SCTV, so we’re always ready to argue over the relative merits of particular seasons. Well, these brother-sister dynamics might be put to the test this year, because SNL just dropped its most polarizing and hilarious sketch in years.

If you haven’t heard about the latest skit, “Sister,” we have the entire thing below. Depending on your perspective, you may laugh nervously, nod vigorously or cry knowingly at the very real situation SNL pokes fun at. Read on for details on the outrageous sketch that’s taking over your social media feed right now and will likely come up at Thanksgiving dinner.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

What is SNL’s “Sister” skit, exactly?

The skit takes the form of a parody infomercial, with host John Mulaney addressing the camera like he’s about to sell you Medicare Part B. Over a backdrop of scenes of his elderly father, played by Tommy Brennan, Mulaney says he loves his dad and doesn’t want to see him go to a nursing home. And live-in care is expensive!

“That’s when I heard about Sister,” he says to the camera. “Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder-care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” To activate, all Mulaney has to do is text: “Dad fell.” Soon, cast member Jane Wickline shows up at their father’s house with a roller bag after quitting her job and breaking her lease.

Other cast members, including Andrew Dismukes and Keenan Thompson, speak to the camera about how much they love their moms, but that doesn’t mean they want to help them in the bathroom or learn about their “confusing” medicines. Sister doesn’t either, “but she will, whereas I won’t,” Dismukes says.

For brothers, it’s a win-win: “Now I don’t have to worry about my dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it,” Mulaney says. “And I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do.”

What was the swift and brutally honest internet reaction?

This skit hit a nerve, to say the least. Long-suffering, real-life “Sisters” took to social media to say they finally feel seen, while brothers and other siblings defended their own situations, which you know nothing about thank you very much!

  • “As a caregiver, the SNL ‘Sister’ skit is actually a documentary,” said one put-upon caretaker on Threads.
  • “Omg, this is so true. I am the sister 😵‍💫,” said someone on Instagram.
  • “The best part are the two ‘Happy Birthday’ texts before ‘dad fell,’ showing how much he communicates with her,” said an observant YouTuber.
  • “Not even satire, a much needed public service announcement on how bad this sucks to be me. Thank you to the writers,” said another.

Sister partners, who also make an appearance in the skit, also related to this modern commentary on caregiving. “Speaking as someone who inadvertently found himself in the role of ‘Sister’s Husband,’ I can attest that this video is 100% accurate,” said someone on the official SNL YouTube channel.

How accurate is this family dynamic in real life?

Very. Studies broadly support the idea that daughters are more likely than sons to take on caregiving roles for aging parents. According to a 2025 study by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 61% of caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men.

One particularly biting part of the skit touches on well-worn societal expectations of daughters. Mikey Day plays a doctor (and author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care), who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours.” And in fact, studies bear this out.

In one study, daughters were three times as likely as sons to have this expectation on them. Daughters also tend to model behavior from previous generations, which keeps the cycle going.

If you’re a brother, what should you do now?

Do something, brothers. Anything. (Like, please!) But seriously, just remember that the “Sister” skit rings true for a reason—your sister is probably facing more caregiving pressures than you. It’s not an indictment of all men, so avoid leaping to your gender’s defense while your older sister is organizing approximately 283 doctor’s appointments for your dad.

And, in general, if you really want to avoid Sister’s wrath, skip saying things like “Mom doesn’t want me to see her like this.” News flash: She doesn’t want your sister to see her that way either.
